rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the crowded early cluster responds to slope. This diagnostic run will distinguish slope-sensitive separations from pairs that need a temperature or starting-composition change.

The shallower gradient improved the early cluster but incurred a time penalty, while one pair improved only modestly. Test higher temperature at the original slope to shift selectivity and shorten retention.

At 60 C only one pair remains below target, and the last peak leaves nearly two minutes before the penalty threshold. Modestly lengthen the gradient to test whether that remaining pair improves while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient instead. The other close pairs currently have enough resolution margin to make this a useful test of faster separation.

The critical pair responds weakly to gradient duration, so shift the starting composition to probe selectivity. The first peak was retained beyond 1.2 minutes at 60 C, giving some room to raise phi0 without forcing it to the dead time.
Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter gradient. Reducing tG by one grid step may preserve full resolution while shortening the separation.
Shorten the gradient one more step to locate the full-resolution boundary. Injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method if the early cluster falls below R = 1.5.

Slightly reduce the gradient span to restore the two marginal early separations at tG = 8 minutes. This gives a slope between injections 7 and 8, with enough final organic strength to keep the last peak within the gradient.

Injection 9 is now the fastest fully resolved benchmark. Test a slightly higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention and shift the early-cluster selectivity, while checking that the first peaks remain sufficiently retained and separated.

Probe temperature-dependent selectivity at the faster gradient, since adjusting phi0 trades resolution between the two early critical pairs. Compare directly with injection 8 while retaining injection 9 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Return to 60 C and test a gradient slope between the fully resolved injection 9 and marginal injection 8. The narrower window should still accommodate the last peak while probing a slightly faster full-resolution boundary.

Test the low-temperature extreme for a different elution order that might resolve the early cluster at this fast slope. Injection 12 still has a marginal pair despite its rounded CRF, so injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved benchmark.

Return to 60 C and combine the improved fourth–fifth separation at phi0 = 0.20 with a shallower gradient to recover the third–fourth pair. This tests an alternative fully resolved operating window while retaining injection 9 as the fastest confirmed benchmark.

Reduce the gradient span one step to bring the remaining R = 1.46 pair above target at phi0 = 0.20. This should establish an alternative fully resolved method comfortably below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

The faster boundary is established near injection 9; now test whether a shallower gradient provides a larger resolution margin while retaining the maximum CRF. Extrapolation places the last peak near 9 minutes, below the time-penalty threshold.

Test the unexamined starting fraction between 0.05 and 0.15 while preserving injection 9’s gradient slope. This isolates the starting-composition effect on the critical cluster and checks for another fully resolved window.

Back off one endpoint step from injection 12 to restore its marginal early pair while keeping the programmed gradient short. The last peak may enter the final hold, but its previously observed elution composition suggests it should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test the remaining endpoint step between fully resolved injection 9 and faster injection 8. This directly checks whether a modest speed gain is possible without losing full resolution; injection 9 remains the benchmark if the critical pair falls short.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 15 to lift its R = 1.49 pair above target and confirm a second fully resolved starting-composition window. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Refine around injection 9 by lowering phi1 one step to give its marginal critical pair more resolution margin. This should retain the maximum CRF with only a small increase in retention time and keep all peaks inside the gradient.

Test an intermediate speed–resolution compromise between injections 7 and 6, using a narrower gradient window. This should preserve maximum CRF with more critical-pair margin than the fastest fully resolved method, injection 9.

Refine the fully resolved region with a slope between injections 7 and 22, aiming for more resolution margin than injection 7 and less retention time than injection 22. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed method achieving the maximum CRF.

Test a narrower eight-minute gradient for additional critical-pair margin while keeping the last peak inside the gradient and below 10 minutes. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved benchmark; this run evaluates a less marginal alternative at the same maximum score.

Use the final injection to test an unrun duration bracketed by fully resolved injections 6 and 16, targeting a larger resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already achieved, and injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
